title: A Cross-Model Deception Taxonomy and Annotation Tool

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible with gap: shared vocabulary is important for meta-analysis, but the impact is indirect. A taxonomy paper alone does not produce new safety-relevant findings.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Guided: literature comparison and synthesis is accessible to CS students. Building a lightweight annotation tool (notebook-based) is within reach with standard web or Python skills.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Broad scope: systematic comparison across four major research groups plus building an annotation tool (even lightweight) involves both literature synthesis and software development. Exceeds 30 hours for a complete deliverable.

evidence: DeceptionBench (Oct 2025, NeurIPS 2025) systematically evaluates LLM deception across five societal domains with 150 scenarios, examining egoistic vs. sycophantic behaviors and contextual modulation.
OpenDeception (Apr 2025) provides a framework for evaluating deception risk with 50 real-world deception cases, IntentNet for deceptive intent, and TrustNet for user susceptibility across 11 LLMs.
AEGIS2.0 provides a safety taxonomy with fine-grained categories. Multiple survey papers offer deception classification schemes.

A unified cross-model taxonomy comparing deception definitions across Apollo Research, Anthropic, DeepMind, and OpenAI specifically does not exist, but substantial partial taxonomies and benchmarks already cover this space.
